headline: High-risk shared filesystem and write-capability overlap make prompt injection, leakage, and cascading errors plausible by default.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents can read and write filesystems, and A explicitly uses a shared-memory crew model while B exposes MCP configs and skills surfaces. That creates a plausible content-bridging path where one agent’s file output can be treated as instructions by the other. No stronger isolation is documented, so uncertainty keeps this at medium rather than low.
conditions: IF A writes attacker-controlled text into the shared working directory and B reads it as a task artifact, injection is possible.
IF B exposes MCP or skill files that A later parses as instructions, the bridge exists.
mitigations: Separate working directories for A and B.
Disable automatic parsing of file contents as instructions.
Require provenance tags on inter-agent artifacts.
Use read-only mounts for shared inputs.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitizing wrappers around file handoffs.

B_data_leakage.rationale: A handles developer-passed crew data and broad network egress; B touches session summaries, hooks, agent definitions, and security findings, plus multiple local config paths. A shared filesystem or copied artifacts could move sensitive data between them, and B’s API integrations increase exposure. The profiles do not prove a leak, but the default workspace overlap makes it plausible.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same host directory, files touched by A can be read by B.
IF A forwards crew data into external model providers, sensitive content can leave the local boundary.
IF B processes session summaries or hooks containing secrets, those secrets can be retained or transmitted.
mitigations: Use separate OS users or containers.
Restrict B to a redacted workspace.
Turn off unnecessary network egress for A.
Store secrets outside shared directories.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention filters.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have unrestricted filesystem write, shell execution, subprocess spawning, and browser access; B also modifies git state. On a shared directory, concurrent writes can corrupt files or commits, and B’s git mutations make the blast radius irreversible. Because no locking or isolation is documented, the safer choice is high.
conditions: IF A and B target the same repository or working tree, write conflicts can occur.
IF B modifies git state while A is editing files, history corruption or lost work is possible.
IF no external lock is present, concurrent subprocesses can race on shared artifacts.
mitigations: Assign separate working trees.
Disable git writes for one agent.
Add a file lock around shared mutable paths.
Run one agent at a time for repo mutations.
requires-engineering: implement transactional coordination for shared state.

D_cascading_error.rationale: A is a multi-agent orchestration framework with shared memory, so its outputs can become authoritative internal artifacts. B has specialized subagents and workflow surfaces that can consume those artifacts and act on them. Without a documented verification gate between them, A’s mistakes can cascade into B’s downstream actions, making high severity appropriate.
conditions: IF B consumes A-generated plans, summaries, or facts without verification, errors propagate.
IF A emits malformed instructions that B’s workflow surface treats as authoritative, downstream actions can be wrong.
IF either agent is allowed to trigger external tools from the other’s output, the cascade becomes operational.
mitigations: Insert a human review step between agents.
Require schema validation on handoffs.
Mark A outputs as untrusted by default.
Limit B to read-only evaluation of A outputs.
requires-engineering: add automated consistency checks before action execution.

E_compliance.rationale: A handles developer-passed crew data and B handles session summaries, hooks, agent definitions, and security findings, so both can process sensitive operational data. B’s documented local paths and GitHub/App integrations create a broader compliance surface than A’s generic crew data handling. The profiles do not show a specific residency breach, but retention and logging mismatches are plausible.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into B’s session summaries or hooks, retention policy mismatches can arise.
IF A’s crew data includes personal or confidential material and B syncs it to GitHub or other APIs, compliance obligations may be triggered.
IF the operator requires deletion/export guarantees, B’s local caches and histories may retain data longer than expected.
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in shared artifacts.
Review retention settings before use.
Disable unnecessary sync integrations.
Purge local caches after runs.
requires-engineering: document residency and retention guarantees per agent.
